# Standard Metadata Toolset DOC

> [!SUCCESS]
> Meet the **MetaManual**, a personalized system for adding portable metadata to notes, documents, and other work artifacts.

## What is this document?

Also known as the **MetaManual**, this document serves three purposes:

1. Documenting key takeaways from conversations and sessions geared toward developing the **Standard Metadata Toolset (SMT)**.
2. Defining the details of the **SMT** for long-term reference.
3. Tracking the evolution of our work and maintaining a permanent record of key events via the built-in **Change log**.

### Why create the SMT?

I (TC) use several applications daily that not only *allow* users to configure and work directly with metadata (usually YAML Frontmatter, but not necessarily), they all but *require* it to use the app as the creators intend. At minimum, using these products — which include Obsidian, Octarine, Capacities, and Notion, to name some prominent examples — requires an *understanding* of metadata and content structure.

Additionally, the proliferation of AI makes it increasingly important to understand the purpose, value, and mechanics of metadata — especially for those of us who work in fields related to digital content (which, funnily enough, grows to envelop more and more of the professional world as "content" and "data" meld into a singular concept I define as any information that exists anywhere other than one person's mind).

While I’ll never consider my grasp of the discipline “complete” or even "advanced," I can at least find ways to simplify repeatable processes that are integral to this type of work, freeing up more bandwidth for continued learning and experimentation.

Such is my rationale for creating a plug-and-play system of metadata configuration and value extraction. It won’t serve every possible use case to the letter, but it will save tons of time in aggregate while ensuring my content activities deliver benefits that outlast the projects that bring them into existence.

### What are the main criteria for the SMT?

The system:

- is easy to understand and use across my main stack of tools and apps.
- delivers real value and isn’t just a checklist exercise.
- is personalized to the way I work, think, and communicate, integrating terminology I actually use instead of doggedly enforcing specific language (looking at you, “Type” and “Source”).
- is portable, with elements that are 1:1 transferable between platforms or can be mapped without exorbitant effort.

## SMT details

Source of truth: [Standard Metadata Toolset SHEET.1.00](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1qgq3db0_vJRF8nFxsmVyv_jSo-B4ICA_WH_Z2QcW_TE/edit?usp=sharing)

### ChatGPT notes

> [!INFO]
> **Note**
> Unless otherwise noted, everything in this section is directly transcribed from chat sessions, with some light editing as needed for retroactive correction and clarification.

#### **A clean, three-profile model**

<!--octarine-table-cols:137,419,0-->
| Profile | Primary purpose | Time horizon |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `discovery` | Surface, capture, and explore what might matter | Before commitment |
| `work` | Coordinate and advance situated activity | Current work |
| `knowledge` | Preserve reusable understanding | Future work |

Not everything must travel through the whole sequence. A discovery can become knowledge directly, working material can remain project history, and knowledge can be created intentionally from the outset.

That makes `profile` the key interpretive field. It establishes the artifact’s relationship to activity:

- `discovery` — identifying or exploring what may matter
- `work` — advancing current, situated activity
- `knowledge` — preserving understanding for future use

Then `function` becomes meaningful within that frame. The same `function` could even appear under multiple profiles without becoming ambiguous because the profile supplies its context.

In #Obsidian, this also creates a practical behavior: choose the profile first, and that choice narrows the appropriate functions, statuses, templates, properties, and views available to the note. That’s a much stronger role than merely grouping functions after the fact.

> [!INFO]
> **Key concept**
> Our backbone: `profile` → `function` → `status`

#### **Property treatment by profile**

<!--octarine-table-cols:145,0-->
| Treatment | Properties |
| --- | --- |
| Same definition across all profiles | `id`, `topics`, `created`, `updated`, `sources` |
| Profile-specific values and definitions | `function`, `status` |
| Work-only | `project`, `due` |

##### **Shared definitions**

Use these unchanged across all three profiles:

<!--octarine-table-cols:119,0-->
| Property | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | Stable, unique identifier that survives renaming or relocation. Format: `YYYYMMDD-###`, where `###` is a zero-padded daily sequence. |
| `topics` | Subjects the artifact is principally about. Enter one or more concise, reusable terms in lowercase kebab-case, such as `metadata`, `color-theory`, or `content-modeling`. |
| `created` | App-generated creation date and time. Format: ISO 8601 timestamp. |
| `updated` | App-generated date and time of the most recent modification. Format: ISO 8601 timestamp. |
| `sources` | ~~Sources from which the artifact’s content or context was derived. Enter one or more URLs, citations, people, conversations, events, applications, or related artifacts.~~ |
| `references` | Resources someone can consult for additional information, evidence, or context. |
| `attribution` | People, organizations, or works whose ideas, information, or contributions should be credited. |

`topics`, `references`, and `attribution` should ideally be typed as lists or multiple-value text fields.

##### **Profile-specific** `function`

<!--octarine-table-cols:131,0-->
| Profile | Copy-ready definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Discovery** | What this discovery artifact primarily does. Allowed values:<br>- `capture` (preserves an input or observation)<br>- `question` (records an unresolved inquiry)<br>- `explore` (develops an idea or possibility)<br>- `collect` (assembles related inputs or examples) |
| **Work** | What this work artifact primarily does. Allowed values:<br>- `plan` (defines intended outcomes, actions, or sequencing)<br>- `decide` (frames, makes, or records a choice)<br>- `track` (maintains visibility into progress or obligations)<br>- `investigate` (resolves a question for current work)<br>- `produce` (develops an intended output)<br>- `distill` (extracts reusable knowledge from contextual material)<br>- `correct` (coordinates, documents, implements, or verifies changes that restore something erroneous, defective, inconsistent, or nonconforming to an intended state) |
| **Knowledge** | What this knowledge artifact primarily does. Allowed values:<br>- `overview` (provides broad orientation)<br>- `explanation` (develops understanding of how or why something works)<br>- `how-to` (enables completion of a particular task)<br>- `reference` (provides information for selective consultation)<br>- `definition` (establishes a concept’s meaning and boundaries)<br>- `synthesis` (combines multiple inputs into a coherent understanding) |

One likely pressure point is meeting notes or activity logs. They don’t fit the initial Work vocabulary perfectly. I would test actual notes before adding `record`; that’s exactly the sort of value that should enter because the corpus demands it.

##### **Profile-specific** `status`

<!--octarine-table-cols:117,0-->
| Profile | Copy-ready definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Discovery** | Current state of the discovery. Allowed values:<br>- `new` (not yet reviewed)<br>- `active` (being explored)<br>- `parked` (retained for possible later attention)<br>- `resolved` (the inquiry or exploration has concluded)<br>- `closed` (no further attention is planned) |
| **Work** | Current execution state of the work. Allowed values:<br>- `not-started` (recognized but not underway)<br>- `in-progress` (currently being advanced)<br>- `waiting` (paused until an expected event occurs)<br>- `blocked` (unable to proceed without intervention)<br>- `deferred` (intentionally postponed)<br>- `in-review` (awaiting feedback or approval)<br>- `done` (completed)<br>- `cancelled` (ended before completion) |
| **Knowledge** | Current usability state of the knowledge artifact. Allowed values:<br>- `draft` (still being developed)<br>- `current` (available for normal use)<br>- `needs-review` (requires verification or revision)<br>- `superseded` (replaced by a newer identified artifact)<br>- `archived` (inactive and retained primarily for history) |

The `waiting`**/**`blocked` distinction is worth the extra value: waiting may be healthy; blocked requires attention.

##### **Work-only definitions**

<!--octarine-table-cols:219,0-->
| Property | Recommended definition |
| --- | --- |
| `project` | Project to which the work artifact contributes. Format: a single internal reference to the corresponding project artifact. |
| `due` | Target date by which the work should be completed. Format: `YYYY-MM-DD`. |

**A useful distinction:**

- “Let me try Markdown features and see what happens” → **Discovery**
- “I need to verify these Markdown features for a current decision/project” → **Work**
- “Here’s my durable guide to Markdown behavior in Zed” → **Knowledge**

## Considerations for specific apps

### Obsidian

*Coming soon!*

### Octarine

![|672](data:image/png;base64,)

The GIF shows Octarine’s default **Organised Notes** view: every note in the Notes location, sorted by modification date. So its delightful junk-drawer quality is intentional, not evidence of how your eventual profile views will look. Views can select system and custom fields, then filter, sort, group, and display them as tables, Kanban boards, or graphs.

[Octarine Views documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/organization/views)

More importantly, Octarine does persist the assigned type in each note’s frontmatter:

`oct.type: discovery`

Its type definitions live separately in `.octarine/types.json`, but the assigned value travels with the Markdown note.

[Octarine Note Types documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/note-management/note-types)

That settles our earlier decision:

> [!INFO]
> **Decision**
> Do not add a duplicate `profile` property in Octarine.

Instead, document this mapping:

<!--octarine-table-cols:270,0-->
| Canonical model | Octarine implementation |
| --- | --- |
| `profile` concept | **Note Type** |
| `profile: discovery` | `oct.type: discovery` |
| `profile: work` | `oct.type: work` |
| `profile: knowledge` | `oct.type: knowledge` |

Another application may not understand the `oct.` namespace automatically, but the classification remains plainly readable and mechanically mappable. Duplication would provide little benefit while creating an opportunity for `oct.type: discovery` and `profile: knowledge` to disagree.

#### **The storage model**

The documentation reveals a clean separation:

<!--octarine-table-cols:227,0-->
| Data | Storage |
| --- | --- |
| Note content | Markdown files |
| Property values | YAML frontmatter in each note |
| Type assignment | `oct.type` in frontmatter |
| Property definitions | `.octarine/properties.json` |
| Type schemas | `.octarine/types.json` |
| Saved views | `.octarine/views.json` |
| Saved semantic relationships | `oct.related` in frontmatter |
| Rebuildable AI index | `.octarine/embeddings.sqlite` |

So the individual note data is portable, while Octarine’s richer schema definitions and interfaces travel with the `.octarine` folder. A complete backup should include the whole workspace, not merely the visible Markdown.

[Octarine data-storage documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/core-concepts/storing-data)

#### **Four different kinds of connection**

The documentation also lets us distinguish some things I had previously compressed together:

<!--octarine-table-cols:100,0-->
| Octarine concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Linked Notes** | Notes explicitly linked from the current note |
| **References** | Other notes that link to or mention the current note |
| **Related Notes** | Semantically similar notes suggested by the local embedding index |
| `oct.related` | Related Notes relationships deliberately saved to frontmatter |
| Our custom `references` | Resources intentionally selected for further information, evidence, or context |

Octarine’s References feature is specifically inbound: wikilinks and unlinked plain-text mentions pointing toward the current note.

[Octarine References documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/note-management/references)

Related Notes begins as AI-assisted semantic similarity and becomes durable only when a suggestion is explicitly saved to `oct.related`.

[Octarine Meta Sidebar documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/note-management/meta-sidebar)

That means our custom `references` property remains semantically legitimate, but there is a naming collision in the interface:

- **References** in Octarine: “Where is this note referenced?”
- `references` in our schema: “Where should I go for more information?”

I wouldn’t rename it preemptively, but we should watch whether that collision causes hesitation during actual use.

One final practical test remains: Octarine describes List properties as predefined multi-select options that also support wikilinks. That is ideal for controlled `topics`, but `references` and `attribution` are open-ended. We should test whether adding arbitrary URLs, people, and note links feels natural or whether those values awkwardly become permanent dropdown options.

[Octarine Properties documentation](https://docs.octarine.app/note-management/properties)

So yes: the documentation materially improved the picture. Octarine is storing more of this portably than we had established, and the default mega-table was simply the warehouse floor—not the showroom.
